\( \def\U{\mathcal{U}} \def\V{\mathcal{V}} \def\W{\mathcal{W}} \)

MATH2040 Linear Algebra II

Vector Space

To discuss vector space, we first need a notion of field. A field $F$ is an abstraction over $\mathbb{R}$, which is an algebraic structure that supports binary operations $+$ (addition) and $\cdot$ (multiplication) as well as their inverses, subtraction and division (dividing non-zero elements). The distributive law also holds for field, that is, $\cdot$ is distributive over $+$.

A vector space is a set of vectors $\mathcal{V}$ over scalar field $F$, equipped with $+: \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V} \rightarrow \mathcal{V}$ and $\cdot: F \times \V \rightarrow \V$ such that $(\vec{x}, \vec{y}) \mapsto \vec{x} + \vec{y}$ and $(a, \vec{x}) \mapsto a \vec{x}$ where $\vec{x}, \vec{y} \in V$, $a \in F$, where the arrow above $x$ is used to denote vectors (omitted when clear). Similar to other algebraic structures, the reason why we introduced this definition is for the sake of abstraction. In fact, vector space generalises the concept of sequences or euclidean space. Examples of vector space includes $F^n$, $M_{m \times n}(F)$ ($m \times n$ matrices), $P(F)$ (polynomials), $F^{\infty}$ (infinite sequences), $\text{Sym}_{n \times n}(F)$ (symmetric matrices) and $\mathcal{F}(S, F)$ (functions from $S$ to $F$).

Vector Subspace

The vector space $\W \subset \V$ is called a subspace of $\V$ whenever $0_\V \in \W$ and is closed under $+$ and $\cdot$. Note that any interesection of subspaces $\bigcap_{\W \in S} \W \subset \V$ is a subspace as well straight from definition.

For subspaces $\U, \W \subset \V$, the sum of $\U$ and $\W$ is defined as $\U + \W = \{ x + y : x \in \U, y \in \W \}$. We denote $\V = \U \oplus \W$ in which $\V$ is the direct sum of $\U$ and $\W$ when $\V = \U + \W$ and $\U \cap \W = \{ 0 \}$, which specially each $v \in \V$ can be uniquely written as $u + w$ with $u \in \U$ and $w \in \W$. Direct sum of multiple subspaces is written as $\U_1 \oplus \U_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus \U_k$. Note that all the above creates new vector subspaces. We can further define projection $\Pi: \U \oplus \W \rightarrow \U$ with $u + w \mapsto u$, which intuitively projects vector in $\U \oplus \W$ onto $\U$.

Linear Independence, Span and Basis

One thing concerning us is - how to represent vector spaces when they contains way too many elements? We want to represent it as a basis set of vectors, which every elements of the vector space can be generated from it uniquely.

Consider a set of vectors $S$. We call $v$ as a linear combination of $S$ when $v = \sum_k a_k \vec{u_k}$ for some $a_k \in F$ and $\vec{u_k} \in S$. Note that the summation is finite, since infinite summation is not well-defined in the abstract sense without convergence! A set $S$ is called linearly independent when $\vec{v} = \vec{0} \implies a_k = 0$ for all $k$, while the span of $S$ is the set of all vectors generated from $S$, that is, $\text{Span}(S) = \langle S \rangle = \{ \sum_k a_k \vec{u_k} : a_k \in F, \vec{u_k} \in S \}$. When $\V = \langle S \rangle$, we say $S$ spans $\V$. When a set $\beta$ is both linear independent and spans $\V$, we say $\beta$ a basis of $\V$.

Interestingly, all the bases of $\V$ has the same cardinality! The replacement theorem states that for finite $S$ which spans $\V$ and linear independent $L$, then $|S| \ge |L|$ and we can pick a subset $H$ of $S$ of size $|S| - |L|$ such that $H \cup L$ spans $\V$, which can be proven with induction. Since bases are both linear independent and spans $\V$, all their cardinality are same, and we may define the dimension of vector space $\dim V$ as the size of any basis.

With bases, we may deduce formulae for dimensions. For example, $\dim \U_1 \oplus \U_2 \oplus \cdots \oplus \U_m = \sum_{i} \dim \U_i$ and $\dim \W_1 + \W_2 = \dim \W_1 + \dim \W_2 - \dim \W_1 \cap \W_2$. If we define the quotient space $\V / \W = \{ v + \W : v \in \V \}$ where $v + \W = \{ v + w : w \in \W \}$ are cosets, then $\dim \V/\W = \dim \V - \dim \W$. Also define the direct product space $\V_1 \times \V_2 = \{ (x, y) : x \in \V_1, y \in \V_2 \}$, then $\dim \V_1 \times \V_2 = \dim \V_1 + \dim \V_2$.

Why must basis of a vector space exists? For finite-dimensional vector space this is apparent, but not so for infinite-dimensional ones. In fact, the existence of basis is guaranteed by Zorn's lemma, which states that if every chain has upper bound, then there exists a maximal element. Thus, we may simply consider the collection of all linear independent sets, then apply Zorn's lemma on it to show existence.

Linear Transformation

A linear transformation is a linear map between vector spaces. Suppose $T: \V \rightarrow \W$. What does it means for $T$ to be "linear"? Intuitively, we have $T(x + y) = T(x) + T(y)$ and $T(a \cdot x) = a \cdot T(x)$ for $x, y \in \V$ and $a \in F$. The set of all linear transformations from $\V$ to $\W$ is denoted as $\mathcal{L}(\V, \W)$. Example includes $T_0$ (zero transformation), $I_\V$ (identity transformation), $L_A : F^n \rightarrow F^m$ (left matrix multiplication).
